title: English v. Trump
lead: An outgoing consumer-finance Director selected a deputy expecting her to succeed him temporarily, while the President chose a different acting Director under the vacancies statute. Both claimed the office, and the deputy asked the district court to stop the President’s designee from serving.

actors.name: Richard Cordray
actors.role: Departing Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

actors.name: Leandra English
actors.role: New Deputy Director claiming statutory authority to act as Director.

actors.name: President Trump
actors.role: President who designated Mulvaney under the vacancies statute.

actors.name: Mick Mulvaney
actors.role: Senate-confirmed Office of Management and Budget Director also designated acting CFPB Director.

proceedings: English sued on November 26, 2017. After an earlier temporary-restraining-order denial, she amended and sought a preliminary injunction. On January 10, 2018, the district court denied that motion for lack of likely success and irreparable harm, with equities also against relief.
limits: This is the January 2018 preliminary-injunction ruling, not a final merits dismissal or the later appeal dismissal. The court assumed without deciding that absence or unavailability included resignation and reserved constitutional and alternative procedural questions. Later CFPB removal decisions are outside this stage.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Cordray appoints a deputy before his resignation takes effect
sections.cue: Why did two officials claim acting authority?
paragraphs: Richard Cordray resigned as Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), effective midnight November 24, 2017, before his five-year term ended. Earlier that day he appointed his chief of staff, Leandra English, Deputy Director effective noon, publicly describing the move as providing orderly succession.

The Dodd-Frank Act provided that the Deputy Director would serve as acting Director during the Director’s absence or unavailability. President Trump instead invoked the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA) to designate Mick Mulvaney, the Senate-confirmed Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). That presidential memorandum took effect at 12:01 a.m. November 26. These were distinct appointments and effective times.

sections.title: The Bureau recognizes Mulvaney while English continues asserting the directorship
sections.cue: What position did the requested injunction seek to change?
paragraphs: The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel and CFPB General Counsel concluded that the FVRA remained available. Senior Bureau management agreed to recognize Mulvaney. On November 27, he began work, received decision requests, and issued directives followed by staff while continuing at OMB.

English continued as Deputy Director and described herself as acting Director in emails and meetings. Mulvaney asked her to stop claiming that role and perform customary deputy duties. He publicly said he was not considering firing her. The dispute concerned authority to exercise the directorship, not an already completed dismissal.

English sued Trump and Mulvaney November 26. After hearings November 27 and 28, Judge Timothy Kelly denied a temporary restraining order. She amended and sought a preliminary injunction December 6; the court heard it December 22. She requested an order restraining any presidential selection other than herself, withdrawing Mulvaney’s designation, and prohibiting his acting service.

sections.title: The statutes provide different mechanisms for temporary service
sections.cue: What did English argue displaced the presidential choice?
paragraphs: The FVRA covered death, resignation, or inability of a Senate-confirmed executive-agency officer. A first assistant ordinarily acted, but §3345(a)(2) allowed presidential selection of another Senate-confirmed officer. Acting service generally lasted up to 210 days, with some nominee restrictions. Section 3347 made this mechanism exclusive unless another statute expressly provided an alternative. Section 3349c excluded certain offices, including appointed members of governing multimember independent bodies.

Dodd-Frank created the CFPB as an independent bureau in the Federal Reserve System, led by a Senate-confirmed Director. At this time the statute provided a five-year term and for-cause removal protection, whose constitutionality was separately before the D.C. Circuit en banc. Section 5491(b)(5) assigned acting service to the Deputy during absence or unavailability. Section 5491(a) applied federal-officer laws unless expressly otherwise provided.

English said the later, specific, mandatory deputy provision displaced the general permissive FVRA. Alternatively, she argued that a serving OMB Director could not lead an independent Bureau. Her Appointments Clause theory likewise depended on absence of statutory designation authority.

sections.title: Kelly finds two compatible routes rather than an implied repeal
sections.cue: Why did the FVRA apply on its own terms?
paragraphs: The CFPB was an executive agency, its Director required Senate confirmation, and Cordray resigned. The multimember exception did not apply merely because the Director also sat on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s board. That seat followed the office automatically; the exception concerned persons appointed to the multimember body by the President with Senate consent. Congress had not added this Director to the exclusions.

Section 3347 made the FVRA nonexclusive when another succession law applied, not unavailable. Hooks, involving the National Labor Relations Board General Counsel, supported that interaction, though its provision predated the FVRA and lacked Dodd-Frank’s exact mandatory language. It was an analogy rather than a conclusive answer.

Dodd-Frank’s own express-statement provision reinforced continued application. This was not an earlier Congress trying to bind a later one; the later Congress specified how existing officer laws applied to the Bureau it was creating. Nothing expressly barred the FVRA. Kelly questioned whether absence or unavailability included permanent resignation but assumed it did without deciding, because that still did not expressly displace presidential authority.

sections.title: The mandatory deputy language retains work without excluding the FVRA
sections.cue: How did the court address specificity and independence?
paragraphs: Read in context, the direction that the Deputy shall serve was a default qualified by presidential FVRA selection. Other mandatory-service provisions coexisted with removal or alternative choices. Harmonious construction and the presumption against implied repeal favored both statutes; later-specific-over-general canons did not settle a conflict that could be reconciled. The FVRA itself specifically addressed resignation.

The deputy provision was not redundant. It did not expressly impose FVRA time or nominee restrictions and could cover temporary absences beyond that statute’s apparent reach. Constitutional avoidance supplied additional support: English’s approach could let an outgoing protected Director choose a successor insulated from presidential control, raising serious Take Care Clause concerns. Kelly did not decide that constitutional question or make avoidance necessary to his textual result. Comparisons with Federal Housing Finance Agency arrangements and judicial appointment of inferior officers did not create broader constitutional rules.

Other independence features remained, including Federal Reserve funding and communication protections. FVRA selection required prior Senate confirmation and limited service, while the deputy had no Senate confirmation. Unexplained deletion of an explicit FVRA reference from an earlier bill supplied little reliable legislative history.

sections.title: Dual service at OMB is not an enacted disqualification
sections.cue: What alternative defenses did Kelly leave aside?
paragraphs: Calling the Bureau independent did not itself prohibit simultaneous OMB service. Congress expressly barred the Director and Deputy from positions in certain financial institutions and regulated entities, without naming OMB. Requirements to provide OMB financial information, while disclaiming mandatory consultation or approval, did not establish a wall barring the appointment.

Mulvaney’s Senate-confirmed OMB position met §3345(a)(2). With English unlikely to succeed on the substantive theory, Kelly reserved the defendants’ separate objections based on the de facto officer doctrine and quo warranto.

sections.title: English also fails to establish personal irreparable harm
sections.cue: Why did preliminary relief fail independently of the statutory reading?
paragraphs: A preliminary injunction required likely success, likely irreparable injury, favorable equities, and public interest; the latter two merged when the Government opposed relief. Kelly did not resolve whether Winter had eliminated the circuit’s earlier sliding scale or whether a mandatory-injunction standard applied. English failed even the less demanding alternatives.

Even assuming her legal theory, she remained employed, faced no identified imminent termination, and submitted no declaration facts establishing personal harm. Berry, involving removed Civil Rights Commissioners and an expiring commission’s unfinished report, was different. The CFPB continued functioning, and injury to it or others did not prove hers. The possibility that a permanent appointment would soon end her chance to serve was speculative.

English had never been uncontested acting Director. The last uncontested position was Deputy, so elevating her by injunction would not merely preserve that status quo. Lack of likely success and lack of irreparable harm each independently supported denial.

sections.title: The existing operating arrangement remains in place pending litigation
sections.cue: What did the January order actually decide?
paragraphs: The equities and public interest likewise favored denial. English asserted a statutory right to act, but Mulvaney asserted the corresponding right and she was unlikely to prevail. The President, Bureau counsel, and senior management recognized him, and operations followed that arrangement. An injunction would disrupt it rather than clarify matters.

On January 10, 2018, Kelly denied the preliminary-injunction motion. No separate opinion was issued. The ruling was neither the earlier temporary-restraint decision nor a final dismissal of every claim. The assigned account’s later July 13, 2018 appeal dismissal was subsequent procedural history, not a new merits ruling made here.
